:::{#thm-diagonalizable}
#### Diagonalizable means a basis of eigenvectors

A $p \times p$ matrix $\matr{A}$ is diagonalizable (@def-diagonalizable)
exactly when it has $p$ linearly independent eigenvectors.
Then $\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}$
with the eigenvectors as the columns of $\matr{X}$
and their eigenvalues, in the same order, on the diagonal of $\matr{\Eigvals}$.

:::

::: proof

Let $\matr{X}$ have columns $\vecf{x}_1, \ldots, \vecf{x}_p$
and $\matr{\Eigvals} = \diag(\eigval_1, \ldots, \eigval_p)$.
Column $j$ of $\matr{A} \matr{X}$ is $\matr{A} \vecf{x}_j$,
and column $j$ of $\matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}$ is $\matr{X}$ times column $j$ of $\matr{\Eigvals}$ (@def-matrix-mult),
which is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{X}\,(\eigval_j \vecf{e}_j) &= \eigval_j\,(\matr{X} \vecf{e}_j) \\
&= \eigval_j \vecf{x}_j
\end{aligned}
$$

(@thm-scalar-matmul, @thm-matvec-columns),
so

$$
\matr{A} \matr{X} = \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}
\iff \matr{A} \vecf{x}_j = \eigval_j \vecf{x}_j \text{ for every } j.
$$ {#eq-ax-xlambda}

Also, $\matr{X}$ has rank $p$ exactly when its $p$ columns are linearly independent (@def-rank),
which by @thm-invertible-rank is exactly when $\matr{X}$ is invertible.

**Eigenvectors give a diagonalization.**
If $\vecf{x}_1, \ldots, \vecf{x}_p$ are linearly independent eigenvectors,
then $\matr{X}$ is invertible and @eq-ax-xlambda gives $\matr{A} \matr{X} = \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}$, so

$$
\ba
\matr{A}
&= \matr{A}\,\matr{I}_p
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\\
&= \matr{A}\,(\matr{X} \matr{X}^{-1})
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= (\matr{A} \matr{X})\,\matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}.
&& \text{(} \matr{A} \matr{X} = \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals} \text{)}
\ea
$$

**A diagonalization gives eigenvectors.**
If $\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}$, then

$$
\ba
\matr{A} \matr{X}
&= (\matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1})\,\matr{X}
&& \text{(substitute } \matr{A} \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}\,(\matr{X}^{-1} \matr{X})
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}\,\matr{I}_p
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals},
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\ea
$$

so each column satisfies $\matr{A} \vecf{x}_j = \eigval_j \vecf{x}_j$ (@eq-ax-xlambda).
$\matr{X}$ is invertible, so its columns are linearly independent,
and in particular nonzero;
they are $p$ linearly independent eigenvectors.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-thm-diagonalizable}
#### Building the diagonalization from eigenvectors

The eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ of $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
are linearly independent (@exm-eigenvectors-independent),
so with $\matr{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\matr{\Eigvals} = \diag(3, 1)$,
$\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}$;
by @rem-similar-both-ways this is the similarity of @exm-similar, with $\matr{X} = \matr{P}$.
Because $\matr{A}$ is symmetric, @thm-spectral even gives such a factorization with orthonormal eigenvectors
(@def-eigendecomposition):
dividing each column of $\matr{X}$ by its length $\sqrt{2}$ gives one.
By contrast, every eigenvector of $\matr{J}$ in @exm-eigenspace has the form $(t, 0)$,
so any two of them are multiples of each other,
and $\matr{J}$ has no two linearly independent eigenvectors:
another way to see that it is not diagonalizable.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-distinct-diagonalizable}
#### Distinct eigenvalues make a matrix diagonalizable

A $p \times p$ matrix with $p$ different eigenvalues is diagonalizable.

:::

::: proof

Choose one eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
These $p$ eigenvectors are linearly independent (@thm-eigenvectors-independent),
so the matrix is diagonalizable (@thm-diagonalizable).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-distinct-diagonalizable}
#### A triangular matrix with distinct diagonal entries

$\matr{U}$ of @exm-eigen-triangular has the three different eigenvalues $2$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $-1$
(@thm-eigen-triangular), so it is diagonalizable,
even though it is not symmetric, so @thm-spectral does not apply to it.
The converse fails: $\matr{I}_2$ is diagonal, hence diagonalizable
($\matr{I}_2 = \matr{I}_2\,\matr{I}_2\,\matr{I}_2^{-1}$),
but has only the eigenvalue $1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-diagonalizable-powers}
#### Powers of a diagonalizable matrix

If $\matr{A} = \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}$ (@def-diagonalizable)
with $\matr{\Eigvals} = \diag(\eigval_1, \ldots, \eigval_p)$,
then for every positive integer $k$,
$\matr{A}^k = \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}^k \matr{X}^{-1}$
and $\matr{\Eigvals}^k = \diag(\eigval_1^k, \ldots, \eigval_p^k)$.

:::

::: proof

**Powers of $\matr{\Eigvals}$.**
If $\matr{D} = \diag(d_1, \ldots, d_p)$ and $\matr{E} = \diag(e_1, \ldots, e_p)$,
with entries $d_{il}$ and $e_{lj}$ (so $d_{ii} = d_i$ and $e_{jj} = e_j$),
entry $(i, j)$ of $\matr{D} \matr{E}$ is $\sum_l d_{il}\,e_{lj}$ (@def-matrix-mult),
where $d_{il} = 0$ unless $l = i$ and $e_{lj} = 0$ unless $l = j$.
For $i \ne j$ no term survives, so the entry is $0$;
for $i = j$ only $l = i$ survives, giving $d_i\,e_i$.
So $\matr{D} \matr{E} = \diag(d_1 e_1, \ldots, d_p e_p)$,
and [induction](proof-writing.qmd#def-proof-by-induction) on $k$ gives $\matr{\Eigvals}^k = \diag(\eigval_1^k, \ldots, \eigval_p^k)$.

**Powers of $\matr{A}$, by induction on $k$.**
$k = 1$ is the assumption. If it holds for $k - 1$,

$$
\ba
\matr{A}^k
&= \matr{A}^{k-1} \matr{A}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-power, @thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}^{k-1} \matr{X}^{-1}\,\matr{A}
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}^{k-1} \matr{X}^{-1}\,\matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(the assumption)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}^{k-1}\,(\matr{X}^{-1} \matr{X})\,\matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}^{k-1}\,\matr{I}_p\,\matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-inverse)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}^{k-1} \matr{\Eigvals} \matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\\
&= \matr{X} \matr{\Eigvals}^{k} \matr{X}^{-1}.
&& \text{(@def-matrix-power)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-diagonalizable-powers}
#### A closed form for the powers

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$,
with $\matr{X}$ as in @exm-thm-diagonalizable and $\matr{X}^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\matr{X}$ (@exm-similar),

$$
\ba
\matr{A}^k
&= \matr{X}\,\diag(3^k, 1)\,\matr{X}^{-1}
&& \text{(@thm-diagonalizable-powers)}
\\
&= \matr{X}\,\diag(3^k, 1)\,(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\matr{X})
&& \text{(substitute } \matr{X}^{-1} \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}\,\matr{X}\,\diag(3^k, 1)\,\matr{X}
&& \text{(@thm-scalar-matmul)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 3^k & 1 \\ 3^k & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-mult, for } \matr{X}\,\diag(3^k, 1) \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 3^k + 1 & 3^k - 1 \\ 3^k - 1 & 3^k + 1 \end{bmatrix}.
&& \text{(@def-matrix-mult)}
\ea
$$

For $k = 2$ this gives $\tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 8 & 10 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$,
which matches $\matr{A}^2$ in @exm-eigen-shift-power.

:::
